title: The Stinky History of Human Hygiene
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of human hygiene, from ancient and animal grooming through combs and lice, bathing traditions (Indus baths, Roman and Middle Eastern bathhouses, medieval and early modern bathing decline), soap and shampoo development, deodorant and antiperspirant marketing (Odorono, James Walter Young), toothbrushes and tooth powders, and antibacterial soap and the hygiene hypothesis. The episode closes with a listener mail about the French phrase "faire du jogging."

segments.title: Tour dates and ticket sales
segments.summary: Announcement of 2023 tour dates in Orlando, Nashville and Atlanta, with pre-sale and on-sale ticket info.

segments.title: Opening banter on showering
segments.summary: Hosts joke about smelling and discuss how often they shower, including Josh's cold showers during a college summer.

segments.title: Hygiene in animals and ancient origins
segments.summary: Introduction to the topic: animals practice hygienic behaviors, and Valerie A. Curtis traces hygiene back to unicellular life. Hygiene has waxed and waned over history, and past people were not uniformly dirty.

segments.title: Ancient hair care, combs and lice
segments.summary: Judith Berman's 1999 paper argues Paleolithic people cut and styled hair and trimmed body hair to combat lice. Lice are discussed along with school lice checks. Early combs, including a Syrian comb from the Bronze Age inscribed for removing lice, and the combing of sebum from hair are covered.

segments.title: Pre-shampoo hair washing and personal anecdotes
segments.summary: Ash and lye were used to wash hair, and French aristocrats powdered hair with flour. Chuck describes coincidences in which things he read about appeared in real life. Discussion of hair, including Native American body hair and the Europeans' claims about it.

segments.title: Body hair removal and sugaring
segments.summary: Hair removal dates to ancient Egypt, including sugaring, a waxing-like technique with a honey-colored paste. Egyptians and later Europeans plucked eyebrows as a beauty standard, and the shaving history of the Gillette safety razor is touched on.

segments.title: Transition to bathing
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before moving on to the history of bathing.

segments.title: Ancient and Roman bathing and bathhouses
segments.summary: Bathing is ancient, seen in elephants and hippos. Mohenjo-daro's bath and sewage systems are noted, along with Roman bathhouses and the estimated sixty thousand bathhouses in Baghdad around 1000 CE. Chuck describes the coed Turkish bath in Hungary and Spa Castle in Queens. Josh says he was raised Southern Baptist and is uncomfortable being naked.

segments.title: Medieval bathing decline and soap origins
segments.summary: Medieval people bathed for health reasons, including digestion, and bathing fell out of favor from the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries in Europe. People instead wore linen undergarments and frilly collars as displays of cleanliness. Scrapers and alcohol were used by King Louis XIV in place of baths. Early soap was made from fat and lye, and vegetable-oil soap came via the Crusades.

segments.title: Ivory soap, river bathing and plumbing
segments.summary: Germ theory and better plumbing spurred bathing. The first shower box dates to the mid-eighteenth century, and the US outpaced Europe in indoor plumbing. Procter and Gamble's floating Ivory soap is tied to river bathing, and the hosts discuss the environmental effects of soap in rivers.

segments.title: Shampoo history and personal hair care
segments.summary: Shampoo was developed by Procter and Gamble, with Dreft as an early synthetic in the 1930s, replacing boiled soap shavings. Hosts discuss how often they wash their hair.

segments.title: Perfume history and rosemary
segments.summary: Ancient perfumes and cosmetics were heavily applied, which mixed with body odor. Alcohol-based perfume from distillation appeared in the thirteenth century, with Queen of Hungary Water scented with rosemary. The hosts discuss rosemary and the miasma theory of disease, including tularemia.

segments.title: Break before deodorant segment
segments.summary: Short break before the deodorant segment.

segments.title: Deodorant and antiperspirant marketing history
segments.summary: Mum, from 1888, was an early commercial deodorant. The first antiperspirant dates to 1903 and uses aluminum salts. Edna Murphy invented Odorono, and copywriter James Walter Young's fear-based ads targeted women and later men, including the Lady's Home Journal ad that drew cancellations and a 113 percent sales increase. Top Flight and Seaforth were marketed to men, and the Who song Odorono is mentioned.

segments.title: Bad breath, toothpaste, toothbrushes and antibacterial soap
segments.summary: Ancient chewing sticks, abrasive tooth powders that damaged enamel, and the hog-bristle toothbrush from China that persisted until nylon in the 1930s are covered. Bad breath was a grounds for divorce in the Talmud. The FDA banned certain antibacterial soap ingredients in 2016. Triclosan and triclocarban are discussed for superbugs and hormone disruption, and hosts share nutrigena and buff puff acne stories.

segments.title: Wrap-up and related episodes
segments.summary: Hosts recap and point listeners to related episodes on perfume, soap, halitosis, porcupines, and the hygiene hypothesis.

segments.title: Listener mail: jogging in France
segments.summary: James writes about a French host father who invited his exchange student Paul to 'faire du jogging,' and was a dedicated sprinter. Chuck explains the phrase.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and the listener mail address.
